mūla.devanāgarī: इन्द्रियार्थेषु वैराग्यम् अनहंकार एव च | जन्म-मृत्यु-जरा-व्याधि-दुःख-दोषानुदर्शनम्
mūla.chapter_position: Chapter 13 (Kṣetra-Kṣetrajña-Vibhāga-Yoga (The Yoga of Distinction Between Field and Field-Knower)), verse 8
mūla.speaker: Krishna

advaita.reading_summary: (reading summary extraction pending; ENABLE_READING_SUMMARIES=true to generate)
advaita.english_rendering: Vairāgya (dispassion) is absence of attachment to sense-objects such as sound, and to enjoyments seen and unseen; anahaṃkāra is the absence of ahaṃkāra (ego). Doṣānudarśana is reflecting on the defect in each of birth, death, old age, disease and sorrow - the passage from the womb, the loss of intellect, strength and lustre in age - or else seeing that each of them is sorrow, not by its own nature but as a cause of sorrow. From that reflection dispassion toward bodily and sensory enjoyments arises, the organs turn toward the inner Self for its vision, and so, being a cause of knowledge, it is called knowledge.
advaita.divergence_note: Śaṅkara offers two parses of duḥkha-doṣa (defect in each item, or sorrow-as-defect) and insists birth and the rest are sorrow only as causes of sorrow; the payoff is the turning of the organs to the pratyag-ātman (inner Self), which is why a mere attitude can be called jñāna.

viśiṣṭādvaita.reading_summary: (reading summary extraction pending; ENABLE_READING_SUMMARIES=true to generate)
viśiṣṭādvaita.english_rendering: Vairāgya toward sense-objects is recoil from objects other than the self, through contemplating their defectiveness. Anahaṃkāra is freedom from taking the non-self body as the self - said by way of example, so that freedom from taking what is not one's own as one's own is also intended. Doṣānudarśana is contemplating that, while one is embodied, the defect whose form is birth, death, old age, disease and sorrow is unavoidable.
viśiṣṭādvaita.divergence_note: Rāmānuja reads anahaṃkāra as not mistaking the body (anātman) for the self, extended to 'mine'-ness over what is not one's own - not Madhusūdana's 'I am the greatest' pride; and he ties the defects specifically to the condition of being embodied (saśarīratva).

bhakti.reading_summary: (reading summary extraction pending; ENABLE_READING_SUMMARIES=true to generate)
bhakti.english_rendering: Further: doṣānudarśana means reflecting again and again on sorrow and defect in birth and the rest - or, alternatively, seeing the defect that has the form of sorrow. The rest is clear.
bhakti.divergence_note: Śrīdhara glosses only the compound, adding the 'again and again' (punaḥ punaḥ) of repeated reflection, and leaves vairāgya and anahaṃkāra as self-evident.

advaita-bhakti.reading_summary: (reading summary extraction pending; ENABLE_READING_SUMMARIES=true to generate)
advaita-bhakti.english_rendering: Vairāgya is a mental state opposed to rāga, of the nature of non-craving, toward sense-objects seen here or heard of in scripture; ahaṃkāra is the pride, arising in the mind even without spoken self-praise, that 'I am the most excellent of all', and its absence is anahaṃkāra. The 'eva' excludes non-connection and 'ca' means conjunction: the combined practice of all twenty, amānitva and the rest, is what is called knowledge, not with even one missing. Repeated reflection on the defect in birth, death's cutting of every vital point, old age's loss of strength and others' contempt, diseases like fever, sorrows born of losing the wanted and meeting the unwanted, and the loathsomeness of a body full of bile, phlegm and filth, serves the vision of the Self by causing dispassion toward objects.
advaita-bhakti.divergence_note: Madhusūdana distinguishes ahaṃkāra (inner pride without outward boasting) from the mānitva of the previous verse, uses 'eva' and 'ca' to argue all twenty means are required together, and adds the body's loathsomeness (kāya-jugupsā) to the defects - more ascetic in tone than Rāmānuja's embodiment-based reading.

post_generation_repairs.root_cause: Chapter 13 commentaries count 35 verses (13.1 = Arjuna's question) but the edition counts 34; payloads paired mūla 13.N with each commentary's 13.N, i.e. the previous verse's bhāṣya for most schools.

so_what_questions: What would change if I honestly pictured my own aging and illness for a few minutes each week?
Is there pride in me that I never voice but that still runs my decisions?
Which things or roles do I treat as 'me' or 'mine' that are not really either?
Can I keep enjoying good things without making my peace depend on them?
Am I working on all my rough edges together, or polishing one and ignoring the rest?
How do I remind myself of what is unavoidable without becoming morbid?

everyday_applications.advaita: A hospice nurse sees decline every day. Instead of numbing herself, she lets each loss she witnesses quietly loosen her grip on status and comfort, and notices that attention then turns inward to what in her is not aging at all.
everyday_applications.viśiṣṭādvaita: A recently retired executive realizes he had taken his job title as his very self and the company's assets as his own. Seeing that being embodied always brings loss, he stops identifying with the body and the badge, and finds the recoil from them is relief rather than grief.
everyday_applications.dvaita: There is no Dvaita reading supplied for this verse, so nothing is offered here rather than an invented application.
everyday_applications.śuddhādvaita: Only a word-gloss is supplied for this verse; the simplest honest application is to name the specific sense-objects - screens, food, purchases - you are trying to hold lightly.
everyday_applications.bhakti: A manager who keeps relapsing into overwork sets a recurring calendar note to reflect again and again on what burnout, illness and age actually cost. A single realization fades; the repeated look is what holds.
everyday_applications.advaita-bhakti: A star surgeon never brags aloud, but inwardly assumes she is the best in the department. She treats that silent pride as its own fault, separate from boasting, and works on it alongside patience and honesty - knowing that fixing one trait while keeping the others does not count.
